A fire at 3 p.m. inside the mechanical room of the John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum, briefly thought to be related to the marathon explosions, was not caused by a device and is apparently not related to them.

Boston police commissioner Edward Davis stated at a press conference at around 6:00 pm, "There is no suspect in custody."

An Muslim Saudi Arabian man has been identified as a suspect.

A fire at 3 p.m. inside the mechanical room of the John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum, briefly thought to be related to the marathon explosions, was not caused by a device and is apparently not related to them.
Boston police commissioner Edward Davis initially stated at a press conference at around 6:00 pm, "There is no suspect in custody."

A Saudi national who was near the scene of the blast is being held in custody in relation to the incident,  CBS later reported.

Investigation.plaintext:
The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Central Intelligence Agency and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

Boston police commissioner Edward Davis said at a 6 p.m. press conference on April 15, "There is no suspect in custody." Following this statement, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings.

Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere. Police pulled over a suspicious driver who drove past the State Police barracks several times after the bombings. They are searched the driver's home because he seemed nervous, according to officials. Some investigators left the residence carrying brown paper bags, plastic trash bags, and a duffel bag.

Police are searching for a rental van and for a hooded man who left the area before the explosions.
 
Two men, not sitting next to one another and speaking Arabic, were escorted off an American Airlines flight headed to Chicago at Logan Airport. Some participants in the marathon on the flight were concerned, so the plane was brought back to the gate.

Police are searching for a Penske rental van and for a hooded man who left the area before the explosions.

A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made of a pressure cooker filled with metal, nails and ball bearings and put in a backpack.

Investigation.plaintext:
The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Central Intelligence Agency and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

Boston police commissioner Edward Davis said at a 6 p.m. press conference on April 15, "There is no suspect in custody." Following this statement, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man tackled by a suspicious civilian and brought to police.

Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, home to a Saudi man, considered a "person of interest", who was injured by shrapnel. Some investigators left the residence carrying brown paper bags, plastic trash bags, and a duffel bag. The Washington Post reported that the individual was being treated as a witness, not a suspect, by law enforcement.

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. Representative Peter King, member of the Intelligence Committee, was quoted as saying, "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

Police are searching for a Penske rental van and for a hooded man who left the area before the explosions.

A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker filled with metal objects, placed in a backpack. A pressure cooker was also used in the 2010 Times Square car bombing attempt and the 2006 Mumbai train bombings.

Investigation.plaintext:
The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Central Intelligence Agency and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

Boston police commissioner Edward Davis said at a 6 p.m. press conference on April 15, "There is no suspect in custody." Following this statement, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man tackled by a suspicious civilian and brought to police.

Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, home to a Saudi man, considered a "person of interest", who was injured by shrapnel. Some investigators left the residence carrying brown paper bags, plastic trash bags, and a duffel bag. The Washington Post reported that the individual was being treated as a witness, not a suspect, by law enforcement. The New York Times also reported that a law enforcement official said that investigators had determined the man had no involvement in the attack.

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. Representative Peter King, member of the Intelligence Committee, was quoted as saying, "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

Police are searching for a Penske rental van and for a hooded man who left the area before the explosions.

A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker filled with metal objects, placed in a backpack. According to English-language terror magazine Inspire, a pressure-cooker bomb is a preferred weapon of al-Qaeda.

Investigation.plaintext:
The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Central Intelligence Agency and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

Boston police commissioner Edward Davis said at a 6 p.m. press conference on April 15, "There is no suspect in custody." Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man tackled by a suspicious civilian and brought to police.

Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, home to a Saudi man, considered a "person of interest", who was injured by shrapnel. Some investigators left the residence carrying brown paper bags, plastic trash bags, and a duffel bag. The Washington Post reported that the individual was being treated as a witness, not a suspect, by law enforcement. The New York Times also reported that a law enforcement official said that investigators had determined the man had no involvement in the attack.

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. Representative Peter King, member of the Intelligence Committee, was quoted as saying, "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

Police are searching for a Penske rental van and for a hooded man who left the area before the explosions.

A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker filled with metal objects, placed in a backpack.

Some investigators left the residence carrying brown paper bags, plastic trash bags, and a duffel bag. The Washington Post reported that the individual was being treated as a witness, not a suspect, by law enforcement. The New York Times also reported that a law enforcement official said that investigators had determined the man had no involvement in the attack.

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. Representative Peter King, member of the Intelligence Committee, was quoted as saying, "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

Police are searching for a Penske rental van and for a hooded man who left the area before the explosions.

Investigation.plaintext:
The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Central Intelligence Agency and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

Boston police commissioner Edward Davis said at a 6 p.m. press conference on April 15, "There is no suspect in custody." Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man tackled by a civilian who thought he was suspicious and held him for police.

Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, home to a Saudi man, considered a "person of interest", who was injured by shrapnel. Some investigators left the residence carrying brown paper bags, plastic trash bags, and a duffel bag. The Washington Post reported that the individual was being treated as a witness, not a suspect, by law enforcement. The New York Times also reported that a law enforcement official said that investigators had determined the man had no involvement in the attack.

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. Representative Peter King, member of the Intelligence Committee, was quoted as saying, "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

Police are searching for a Penske rental van and for a hooded man who left the area before the explosions.

A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb.

On April 16, 2013, President Barack Obama said that the bombings were being investigated as an act of terror, but authorities still didn't know who is responsible. Obama called the bombing "a heinous and cowardly act used to target innocent civilians."

Investigation.plaintext:
The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Central Intelligence Agency and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

Boston police commissioner Edward Davis said at a 6 p.m. press conference on April 15, "There is no suspect in custody." Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man tackled by a civilian who thought he was suspicious and held him for police. Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, considered a "person of interest", who was injured by shrapnel. Some investigators left the residence carrying brown paper bags, plastic trash bags, and a duffel bag. The Washington Post reported that the individual was being treated as a witness, not a suspect, by law enforcement. The New York Times also reported that a law enforcement official said that investigators had determined the man had no involvement in the attack.

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee, was quoted as saying, "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb.

On April 16, 2013, President Barack Obama said that the bombings were being investigated as an act of terror, but authorities still didn't know who was responsible. Obama called the bombing "a heinous and cowardly act used to target innocent civilians."

Investigation.plaintext:
thumb|Hazmat workers near the scene
thumbnail|left|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

Boston police commissioner Edward Davis said at a 6 p.m. press conference on April 15, "There is no suspect in custody." Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". Some investigators left the residence carrying brown paper bags, plastic trash bags, and a duffel bag. The Washington Post reported that the individual was being treated as a witness, not a suspect, by law enforcement. The New York Times also reported that a law enforcement official said that investigators had determined the man had no involvement in the attack.

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb.  U.S. Representative Mike McCaul, Chairman of the House Homeland Security Committee, said that "most likely gun powder" was used in the explosive devices.

On April 16, 2013, President Barack Obama said that the bombings were being investigated as an act of terror, but authorities still did not know who was responsible. Obama called the bombing "a heinous and cowardly act used to target innocent civilians."

Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". Some investigators left the residence carrying brown paper bags, plastic trash bags, and a duffel bag. The Washington Post reported that the individual was being treated as a witness, not a suspect, by law enforcement. CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop.  Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb.  U.S. Representative Mike McCaul, Chairman of the House Homeland Security Committee, said that "most likely gun powder" was used in the explosive devices.

On April 16, President Barack Obama said that the bombings were being investigated as an act of terror, but authorities still did not know who was responsible. Obama called the bombing "a heinous and cowardly act used to target innocent civilians."

Investigation.plaintext:
thumb|Hazmat workers near the scene
thumbnail|left|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest".  The Washington Post reported that the individual was being treated as a witness, not a suspect, by law enforcement. CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop.  Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb.  U.S. Representative Mike McCaul, Chairman of the House Homeland Security Committee, said that "most likely gun powder" was used in the explosive devices.

On April 16, President Barack Obama said that the bombings were being investigated as an act of terror, but authorities still did not know who was responsible. Obama called the bombing "a heinous and cowardly act used to target innocent civilians."

Slate  reports that Internet-based crowd-sourced vigilante investigations have begun on Reddit to identify individuals in photographs carrying bags similar to those identified as holding one of the bombs or similar to bags observed alone on the ground..  The Atlantic has published a criticism of this activity.

Investigation.plaintext:
thumb|Hazmat workers near the scene

Investigators believe they have identified a suspect, a source who has been briefed on the investigation told CNN's John King. 

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". The Washington Post reported that the individual was being treated as a witness, not a suspect, by law enforcement. CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media

A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. U.S. Representative Mike McCaul, Chairman of the House Homeland Security Committee, said that "most likely gun powder" was used in the explosive devices.

On April 16, President Barack Obama said that the bombings were being investigated as an act of terror, but authorities still did not know who was responsible. Obama called the bombing "a heinous and cowardly act used to target innocent civilians."

Investigation.plaintext:
thumb|Hazmat workers near the scene

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". The Washington Post reported that the individual was being treated as a witness, not a suspect, by law enforcement. CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media

A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. U.S. Representative Mike McCaul, Chairman of the House Homeland Security Committee, said that "most likely gun powder" was used in the explosive devices.

On April 16, President Barack Obama said that the bombings were being investigated as an act of terror, but authorities still did not know who was responsible. Obama called the bombing "a heinous and cowardly act used to target innocent civilians."

Investigation.plaintext:
thumb|Hazmat workers near the scene

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". The Washington Post reported that the individual was being treated as a witness, not a suspect, by law enforcement. CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media

A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. U.S. Representative Mike McCaul, Chairman of the House Homeland Security Committee, said that "most likely gun powder" was used in the explosive devices.

On April 16, President Barack Obama said that the bombings were being investigated as an act of terror, but authorities still did not know who was responsible. Obama called the bombing "a heinous and cowardly act used to target innocent civilians."

Investigation.plaintext:
thumb|Hazmat workers near the scene

An arrest was made on April 17, based on video from a Lord and Taylor store. 

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". The Washington Post reported that the individual was being treated as a witness, not a suspect, by law enforcement. CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media

A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. U.S. Representative Mike McCaul, Chairman of the House Homeland Security Committee, said that "most likely gun powder" was used in the explosive devices.

On April 16, President Barack Obama said that the bombings were being investigated as an act of terror, but authorities still did not know who was responsible. Obama called the bombing "a heinous and cowardly act used to target innocent civilians."

Investigation.plaintext:
thumb|Hazmat workers near the scene

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". The Washington Post reported that the individual was being treated as a witness, not a suspect, by law enforcement. CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media

A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. U.S. Representative Mike McCaul, Chairman of the House Homeland Security Committee, said that "most likely gun powder" was used in the explosive devices.

CNN's John King reported Boston officials have confirmed they have a suspect in custody. Lord and Taylor video surveillance may have been key to catching the suspect. Janet Wu of WCVB also confirmed that Boston Police have a suspect in custody.

On April 16, President Barack Obama said that the bombings were being investigated as an act of terror, but authorities still did not know who was responsible. Obama called the bombing "a heinous and cowardly act used to target innocent civilians."

Investigation.plaintext:
thumb|Hazmat workers near the scene

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". The Washington Post reported that the individual was being treated as a witness, not a suspect, by law enforcement. CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media

A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. U.S. Representative Mike McCaul, Chairman of the House Homeland Security Committee, said that "most likely gun powder" was used in the explosive devices.

CNN's John King reported Boston officials have confirmed they have a suspect in custody. Lord and Taylor video surveillance may have been key to catching the suspect. Janet Wu of WCVB also confirmed that Boston Police have a suspect in custody.

On April 16, President Barack Obama said that the bombings were being investigated as an act of terror, but authorities still did not know who was responsible. Obama called the bombing "a heinous and cowardly act used to target innocent civilians."

Investigation.plaintext:
thumb|Hazmat workers near the scene

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". The Washington Post reported that the individual was being treated as a witness, not a suspect, by law enforcement. CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media

A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. U.S. Representative Mike McCaul, Chairman of the House Homeland Security Committee, said that "most likely gun powder" was used in the explosive devices.
An arrest has been made 
On April 16, President Barack Obama said that the bombings were being investigated as an act of terror, but authorities still did not know who was responsible. Obama called the bombing "a heinous and cowardly act used to target innocent civilians."

Investigation.plaintext:
thumb|Hazmat workers near the scene

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". The Washington Post reported that the individual was being treated as a witness, not a suspect, by law enforcement. CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media

A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. U.S. Representative Mike McCaul, Chairman of the House Homeland Security Committee, said that "most likely gun powder" was used in the explosive devices.

On April 16, President Barack Obama said that the bombings were being investigated as an act of terror, but authorities still did not know who was responsible. Obama called the bombing "a heinous and cowardly act used to target innocent civilians."

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". The Washington Post reported that the individual was being treated as a witness, not a suspect, by law enforcement. CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media

A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. U.S. Representative Mike McCaul, Chairman of the House Homeland Security Committee, said that "most likely gun powder" was used in the explosive devices.

On April 16, President Barack Obama said that the bombings were being investigated as an act of terror, but authorities still did not know who was responsible. Obama called the bombing "a heinous and cowardly act used to target innocent civilians."

Investigation.plaintext:
thumb|Hazmat workers near the scene

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". The Washington Post reported that the individual was being treated as a witness, not a suspect, by law enforcement. CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media

A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. U.S. Representative Mike McCaul, Chairman of the House Homeland Security Committee, said that "most likely gun powder" was used in the explosive devices.

On April 16, President Barack Obama said that the bombings were being investigated as an act of terror, but authorities still did not know who was responsible. Obama called the bombing "a heinous and cowardly act used to target innocent civilians." WCVB, CNN, and ABC News News have all confirmed with Boston Police that  a suspect has been arrested and is being taken to Boston Federal Courthouse.An arrest has been made

Investigation.plaintext:
thumb|Hazmat workers near the scene

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". The Washington Post reported that the individual was being treated as a witness, not a suspect, by law enforcement. CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media

A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. U.S. Representative Mike McCaul, Chairman of the House Homeland Security Committee, said that "most likely gun powder" was used in the explosive devices.

On April 16, President Barack Obama said that the bombings were being investigated as an act of terror, but authorities still did not know who was responsible. Obama called the bombing "a heinous and cowardly act used to target innocent civilians."

thumb|Hazmat workers near the scene

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". The Washington Post reported that the individual was being treated as a witness, not a suspect, by law enforcement. CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media

A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. U.S. Representative Mike McCaul, Chairman of the House Homeland Security Committee, said that "most likely gun powder" was used in the explosive devices.

On April 16, President Barack Obama said that the bombings were being investigated as an act of terror, but authorities still did not know who was responsible. Obama called the bombing "a heinous and cowardly act used to target innocent civilians."

thumb|Hazmat workers near the scene

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". The Washington Post reported that the individual was being treated as a witness, not a suspect, by law enforcement. CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media

A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. U.S. Representative Mike McCaul, Chairman of the House Homeland Security Committee, said that "most likely gun powder" was used in the explosive devices.

On April 16, President Barack Obama said that the bombings were being investigated as an act of terror, but authorities still did not know who was responsible. Obama called the bombing "a heinous and cowardly act used to target innocent civilians."

Investigation.plaintext:
thumb|Hazmat workers near the scene

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". The Washington Post reported that the individual was being treated as a witness, not a suspect, by law enforcement. CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media

The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. U.S. Representative Mike McCaul, Chairman of the House Homeland Security Committee, said that "most likely gun powder" was used in the explosive devices.

Investigation.plaintext:
thumb|Hazmat workers near the scene

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". The Washington Post reported that the individual was being treated as a witness, not a suspect, by law enforcement. CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media

A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. U.S. Representative Mike McCaul, Chairman of the House Homeland Security Committee, said that "most likely gun powder" was used in the explosive devices.

On April 16, President Barack Obama said that the bombings were being investigated as an act of terror, but authorities still did not know who was responsible. Obama called the bombing "a heinous and cowardly act used to target innocent civilians."

On April 17, after false reports, starting on CNN that an arrest had been made, the FBI issued at statement saying no arrests had been made and cautioning all news outlets not to be reckless, stating, "these stories often have unintended consequences".

On April 17, after false reports originating on [[CNN]] and very widely reported in other media that an arrest had been made, the FBI issued a statement saying no arrests had been made and cautioning all news outlets not to be reckless, saying "these stories often have unintended consequences".<ref>{{cite web|title=Boston Marathon explosions: Live updates|url=http://www.washingtonpost.com/blogs/early-lead/wp/2013/04/17/boston-marathon-explosions-live-updates/?Post+generic=%3Ftid%3Dsm_twitter_washingtonpost#liveblog-entry-12490|publisher=Washington Post|accessdate=April 17, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=DOJ: No arrest made in Boston bombing|url=http://www.hlntv.com/article/2013/04/17/suspect-boston-marathon-bombing-caught-tape|publisher=HLNTV|accessdate=April 17, 2013}}</ref>

Investigation.plaintext:
thumb|Hazmat workers near the scene

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

The FBI reports that this pressure cooker fragment is part of one of the explosive devices|thumb|left
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media

A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. U.S. Representative Mike McCaul, Chairman of the House Homeland Security Committee, said that "most likely gun powder" was used in the explosive devices. 

On April 16, President Barack Obama said that the bombings were being investigated as an act of terror, but authorities still did not know who was responsible. Obama called the bombing "a heinous and cowardly act used to target innocent civilians."

On April 17, after false reports originating on CNN that an arrest had been made, the FBI issued a statement saying no arrests had been made and cautioning all news outlets not to be reckless, saying "these stories often have unintended consequences".

thumb|Hazmat workers near the scene

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

The FBI reports that this pressure cooker fragment is part of one of the explosive devices|thumb|left
A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the explosion had been discovered.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images of two suspects carrying black backpacks and with their faces visible, each suspect separately at the scene of one of the two explosions.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

The FBI reports that this pressure cooker fragment is part of one of the explosive devices|thumb|left

The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.

Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. thumb|Hazmat workers near the scene

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

The FBI reports that this pressure cooker fragment is part of one of the explosive devices|thumb|left
A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

The FBI reports that this pressure cooker fragment is part of one of the explosive devices|thumb|left
A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.

Investigation.plaintext:
thumb|Hazmat workers near the scene

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

The FBI reports that this pressure cooker fragment is part of one of the explosive devices|thumb|left
A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.
