The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

Suspects.plaintext:
On April 18 at around 5:20 P.M. EDT, the FBI released in a news conference photos and a video of two suspects and sought the public's help in identifying them. According to the FBI, one of the men pictured was seen placing a backpack at the scene minutes before the second bomb exploded. A MorphoTrust USA Inc. official, a company that supplies facial-recognition software to U.S. agencies, said the FBI likely tried running the images through photo databases and didn't get a match. 

During the morning of April 19th, after a car chase, one suspect was captured, while another was still being searched for in the Watertown/Cambridge area. It is unknown if they were part of the shooting death of a police officer at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology or the robbery of two convenience stores nearby.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.

thumb|Hazmat workers near the scene

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

The FBI reports that this pressure cooker fragment is part of one of the explosive devices|thumb|left
A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.

According to the FBI, one of the men pictured was seen placing a backpack at the scene minutes before the second bomb exploded. Chechens from the Russian Caucasus, the two immigrated to the United States in c. 2000–2001. Tamerlan Tsarnaev, who presented himself as a devout Muslim, was killed during a massive manhunt launched in the early hours of April 19. Dzhokhar Tsarnaev posted links to websites about Islam and Chechen separatism on his page on a social networking service.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

The FBI reports that this pressure cooker fragment is part of one of the explosive devices|thumb|left
A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.

False reports of arrests

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.

Tamerlan Tsarnaev, who presented himself as a devout Muslim, was killed during a massive manhunt launched in the early hours of April 19. Dzhokhar Tsarnaev (born July 22, 1993) posted links to websites about Islam and Chechen separatism on his page on a Russian social networking service, VKontakte. On his page, he listed his languages as English, Russian and Chechen; his worldview was given as "Islam." According to his VKontakte account, he graduated from School No. 1 in Makhachkala in 2001, and graduated from Cambridge Rindge and Latin School in 2011. A good student, he received a $2,500 scholarship to attend college from the city of Cambridge the year he graduated; he had also been named a wrestling all-star the same year.

thumb|Dzhokhar Tsarnayev, the remaining, living suspect in the bombingsIn a news conference held at around 5:20 p.m. on April 18, the FBI released photos and a video of two suspects and sought the public's help in identifying them. According to the FBI, one of the men pictured was seen placing a backpack at the scene minutes before the second bomb exploded. Authorities identified two brothers, 26-year-old Tamerlan Tsarnayev (Тамерлан Царнаев) and 19-year-old Dzhokhar Tsarnayev (Джохар Царнаев), as suspects. Chechens from the Russian Caucasus, the two immigrated to the United States in 2000 or 2001.

Tamerlan Tsarnaev, who presented himself as a devout Muslim, was killed during a massive manhunt launched in the early hours of April 19. 

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev (born July 22, 1993) posted links to websites about Islam and Chechen separatism on his page on a Russian social networking service, VKontakte. On his page, he listed his languages as English, Russian and Chechen; his worldview was given as "Islam." According to his VKontakte account, he graduated from School No. 1 in Makhachkala in 2001, and graduated from Cambridge Rindge and Latin School in 2011. A good student, he received a $2,500 scholarship to attend college from the city of Cambridge the year he graduated; he had also been named a wrestling all-star the same year.

King|Peter King]], member of the [[United States House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence|House Intelligence Committee]] said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."<ref>{{cite web|title=Live updates: Obama calls Boston bombings a 'heinous, cowardly' act of terror |url= http://www.latimes.com/news/nation/nationnow/la-na-nn-boston-searches-for-clues-to-bombing-that-killed-3-injured-176-20130416,0,318317.story?page=2 |work=LA Times|accessdate=April 16, 2013}}</ref>

Murphy]], told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.washingtonpost.com/world/national-security/security-video-may-show-boston-marathon-bomb-suspect-report-of-arrest-premature/2013/04/17/2be1a3f6-a78b-11e2-b029-8fb7e977ef71_story.html|title= Security video may show Boston Marathon bomb suspect; report of arrest premature |author = David Montgomery |author2 = Marc Fisher|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=April 17, 2013|accessdate=April 18, 2013}}</ref> Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.<ref>{{cite news|title=Videos Said to Show Clear Images of 2 Bombing Suspects|url=http://www.nytimes.com/2013/04/19/us/boston-set-to-mourn-bombing-victims.html?hp&_r=0|accessdate=April 18, 2013|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=April 18, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Authorities have clear video images of two suspects|url=http://bostonglobe.com/metro/2013/04/18/authorities-have-clear-video-images-two-suspects/YejgNWAcmChcx2lUXigs5I/story.html|accessdate=April 18, 2013|newspaper=[[The Boston Globe]]|date=April 18, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Video images yield two possible Boston bombing suspects|url=http://www.latimes.com/news/nationworld/nation/la-na-boston-bombings-investigation-20130418,0,2651203.story|accessdate=April 18, 2013|newspaper=[[The Los Angeles Times]]|date=April 18, 2013}}</ref>

===False reports of arrests===
On April 17, false reports that an arrest had been made originated on AP and CNN and were repeated in other media. The FBI issued a statement saying that there had been no arrests and cautioning news outlets not to be reckless, saying "these stories often have unintended consequences".

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

The FBI reports that this pressure cooker fragment is part of one of the explosive devices|thumb|left
A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.

False reports of arrests
On April 17, false reports that an arrest had been made originated on AP and CNN and were repeated in other media. The FBI issued a statement saying that there had been no arrests and cautioning news outlets not to be reckless, saying "these stories often have unintended consequences".

Suspect photos released

The FBI has released photo and videos of 2 suspects and is seeking the public's help in identifying them.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

Chechens from the Russian Caucasus, the two immigrated to the United States in 2000 or 2001.

He received a $2,500 scholarship to attend college from the city of Cambridge the year he graduated; he had also been named a wrestling all-star the same year.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

The FBI reports that this pressure cooker fragment is part of one of the explosive devices|thumb|left
A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.

False reports of arrests
On April 17, false reports that an arrest had been made originated on AP and CNN and were repeated in other media. The FBI issued a statement saying that there had been no arrests and cautioning news outlets not to be reckless, saying "these stories often have unintended consequences".

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.

At the time of the incident, he was a student at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth with a major in marine biology.

thumb|Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, the remaining, living suspect in the bombingsIn a news conference held at around 5:20 p.m. on April 18, the FBI released photos and a video of two suspects and sought the public's help in identifying them. According to the FBI, one of the men pictured was seen placing a backpack at the scene minutes before the second bomb exploded. Authorities identified two brothers, 26-year-old Tamerlan Tsarnaev () and 19-year-old Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev (), as suspects. Chechens from the Russian Caucasus, the two immigrated to the United States in 2000 or 2001.

Tamerlan Tsarnaev (), who presented himself as a devout Muslim, was killed during a massive manhunt launched in the early hours of April 19. 

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev () posted links to websites about Islam and Chechen separatism on his page on VKontakte, a Russian social networking service. On his page, he listed his languages as English, Russian and Chechen; his worldview was given as "Islam" and his Personal priority was "career and money". According to his VKontakte account, he attended School No. 1 in Makhachkala, Dagestan, Russia, in 2001, and graduated from Cambridge Rindge and Latin School in 2011. Classmates and acquaintances described him as a kind, sociable individual who was well-integrated into his school community and was "very relaxed" in contrast to his elder brother. He received a $2,500 scholarship to attend college from the city of Cambridge the year he graduated; he had also been named a wrestling all-star the same year.  At the time of the incident, he was a student at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth with a major in marine biology.

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative [[Peter T. King|Peter King]], member of the [[United States House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence|House Intelligence Committee]] said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."<ref>{{cite web|title=Live updates: Obama calls Boston bombings a 'heinous, cowardly' act of terror |url= http://www.latimes.com/news/nation/nationnow/la-na-nn-boston-searches-for-clues-to-bombing-that-killed-3-injured-176-20130416,0,318317.story?page=2 |work=LA Times|accessdate=April 16, 2013}}</ref>

The president of Boston's City Council, [[Stephen J. Murphy]], told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.washingtonpost.com/world/national-security/security-video-may-show-boston-marathon-bomb-suspect-report-of-arrest-premature/2013/04/17/2be1a3f6-a78b-11e2-b029-8fb7e977ef71_story.html|title= Security video may show Boston Marathon bomb suspect; report of arrest premature |author = David Montgomery |author2 = Marc Fisher|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=April 17, 2013|accessdate=April 18, 2013}}</ref> Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.<ref>{{cite news|title=Videos Said to Show Clear Images of 2 Bombing Suspects|url=http://www.nytimes.com/2013/04/19/us/boston-set-to-mourn-bombing-victims.html?hp&_r=0|accessdate=April 18, 2013|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=April 18, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Authorities have clear video images of two suspects|url=http://bostonglobe.com/metro/2013/04/18/authorities-have-clear-video-images-two-suspects/YejgNWAcmChcx2lUXigs5I/story.html|accessdate=April 18, 2013|newspaper=[[The Boston Globe]]|date=April 18, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Video images yield two possible Boston bombing suspects|url=http://www.latimes.com/news/nationworld/nation/la-na-boston-bombings-investigation-20130418,0,2651203.story|accessdate=April 18, 2013|newspaper=[[The Los Angeles Times]]|date=April 18, 2013}}</ref>

thumb|Hazmat workers near the scene

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

The FBI reports that this pressure cooker fragment is part of one of the explosive devices|thumb|left
A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.

False reports of arrests
On April 17, false reports that an arrest had been made originated on AP and CNN and were repeated in other media. The FBI issued a statement saying that there had been no arrests and cautioning news outlets not to be reckless, saying "these stories often have unintended consequences".

Suspect photos released

The FBI has released photo and videos of 2 suspects and is seeking the public's help in identifying them.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.

thumb|Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, the surviving 19-year-old suspect in the bombingsIn a news conference held at around 5:20 p.m. on April 18, the FBI released photos and a video of two suspects and sought the public's help in identifying them. According to the FBI, one of the men pictured was seen placing a backpack at the scene minutes before the second bomb exploded. Authorities identified two brothers, 26-year-old Tamerlan Tsarnaev () and 19-year-old Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev  (), as suspects. Chechens from the Russian Caucasus, the two immigrated to the United States in 2000 or 2001. They have been living in Cambridge, Massachusetts for the last year.

Tamerlan Tsarnaev (October 21, 1986 – April 19, 2013), who presented himself as a devout Muslim, was killed during a massive manhunt launched in the early hours of April 19. 

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev (born July 22, 1993) posted links to websites about Islam and Chechen separatism on his page on VKontakte, a Russian social networking service. On his page, he listed his languages as English, Russian and Chechen; his worldview was given as "Islam" and his personal priority was "career and money". According to his VKontakte account, he attended School No. 1 in Makhachkala, Dagestan, Russia, in 2001, and graduated from Cambridge Rindge and Latin School in 2011. Classmates and acquaintances described him as a kind, sociable individual who was well-integrated into his school community and was "very relaxed." He received a $2,500 scholarship to attend college from the city of Cambridge the year he graduated; he had also been named a wrestling all-star the same year.  At the time of the incident, he was a student at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth with a major in marine biology.

thumb|Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, the 19-year-old suspect currently at largeIn a news conference held at around 5:20 p.m. on April 18, the FBI released photos and a video of two suspects and sought the public's help in identifying them. According to the FBI, one of the men pictured was seen placing a backpack at the scene minutes before the second bomb exploded. Authorities identified two brothers, 26-year-old Tamerlan Tsarnaev () and 19-year-old Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev  (), as suspects. Chechens from the Russian Caucasus, the two immigrated to the United States in 2000 or 2001.  They have been living in Cambridge, Massachusetts for the last year.

Tamerlan Tsarnaev (October 21, 1986 – April 19, 2013), who presented himself as a devout Muslim, was killed during a massive manhunt launched in the early hours of April 19. 

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev (born July 22, 1993) posted links to websites about Islam and Chechen separatism on his page on VKontakte, a Russian social networking service. On his page, he listed his languages as English, Russian and Chechen; his worldview was given as "Islam" and his personal priority was "career and money". According to his VKontakte account, he attended School No. 1 in Makhachkala, Dagestan, Russia, in 2001, and graduated from Cambridge Rindge and Latin School in 2011. Classmates and acquaintances described him as a kind, sociable individual who was well-integrated into his school community and was "very relaxed." He received a $2,500 scholarship to attend college from the city of Cambridge the year he graduated; he had also been named a wrestling all-star the same year.  At the time of the incident, he was a student at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth with a major in marine biology.

[[File:Hazmat biohazard team at Boston Marathon near the finish line 07.jpeg|thumb|[[Dangerous goods|Hazmat]] workers near the scene]]

The [[Federal Bureau of Investigation]], which is investigating the attack along with the [[Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives]] (ATF), the [[Central Intelligence Agency]], and the [[National Counterterrorism Center]],<ref name= "Hosenball">{{cite web| url= http://www.globalpost.com/dispatch/news/thomson-reuters/130415/investigators-scour-video-photos-boston-marathon-bomb-clues |title= Investigators scour video, photos for Boston Marathon bomb clues|last1= Hosenball| first1=Mark |first2= Svea| last2=Herbst-Bayliss |date=April 16, 2013|work= [[GlobalPost]]|publisher= [[Thomson Reuters]] |accessdate =April 16, 2013}}</ref> is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.<ref name="Fox News1"/>

[[File:FBI and JTTF at Boston bombing.jpg|thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media]]
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner [[Edward F. Davis]] told reporters that no suspect was in custody.<ref name="Hunter">{{cite web|url=http://livewire.talkingpointsmemo.com/entry/boston-police-commissioner-there-is-no-suspect-in|title=Boston several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into [[Police custody|custody]] and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable".<ref>{{cite web|title=Injured Saudi man not a suspect in Boston attacks|url=http://www.cbsnews.com/8301-201_162-57579893/sources-injured-saudi-man-not-a-suspect-in-boston-attacks/|last=Sison |first=Bree|publisher=CBS News|accessdate=April 17, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Nelson|first=Steven|title=Boston Police: 'We Are Questioning Many People'|url=http://www.usnews.com/news/newsgram/articles/2013/04/15/boston-police-we-are-questioning-many-people |accessdate=April 16, 2013|newspaper=[[U.S. News & World Report]]}}</ref> Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of [[Revere, Massachusetts |Revere]], the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest".<ref name="Fox News1"/><ref>{{cite news|title=Large police presence in Revere connected to Boston bombing|url= http://www.myfoxboston.com/story/21986273/large-police-presence-in-revere-connected-to-boston-bombing |publisher=[[WFXT]]|accessdate=April 16, 2013}}</ref> CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."<ref name="CNN_FBI">{{cite web|title=FBI will try to rebuild Boston bombs|url=http://www.cnn.com/2013/04/15/us/boston-marathon-investigation/index.html|last=Smith |first=Matt|coauthors=Josh Levs|publisher=CNN|accessdate=April 17, 2013}}</ref>

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative [[Peter T. King|Peter King]], member of the [[United States House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence|House Intelligence Committee]] said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."<ref>{{cite web|title=Live updates: Obama calls Boston bombings a 'heinous, cowardly' act of terror |url= http://www.latimes.com/news/nation/nationnow/la-na-nn-boston-searches-for-clues-to-bombing-that-killed-3-injured-176-20130416,0,318317.story?page=2 |work=LA Times|accessdate=April 16, 2013}}</ref>

[[File:Pressure cooker bomb.jpg|The FBI reports that this pressure cooker fragment is part of one of the explosive devices|thumb|left]]
A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a [[pressure cooker]] packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a [[backpack]].<ref name="CNN_FBI"/> The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop.<ref>{{cite news|last=Ellement|first=John|title=Boston Medical Center reports five-year-old boy in critical condition, 23 victims treated from Boston Marathon bombings|url=http://www.boston.com/metrodesk/2013/04/17/boston-medical-center-reports-five-year-old-boy-critical-condition-victims-treated-from-boston-marathon-bombings/gkKXBTqL2jyNhsC2Kz5GyO/story.html|accessdate=April 17, 2013|newspaper=The Boston Globe|date=April 17, 2013|author2=Brian Ballou}}</ref> Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb.<ref>{{cite news|url= http://www.cbsnews.com/8301-201_162-57579766/boston-marathon-bombings-suburban-apartment-searched/ |title=FBI seeks images in Boston Marathon bomb probe; new details emerge on explosives |work =CBS News|date=April 16, 2013|accessdate=April 16, 2013}}</ref> Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.<ref name="Lister">{{cite web|url=http://edition.cnn.com/2013/04/16/us/boston-marathon-lone-wolf/|title=Boston Marathon bombs similar to 'lone wolf' devices, experts say|last=Lister|first=Tim|coauthors=Paul Cruickshank|date=April 17, 2013|work=[[CNN]]|accessdate=April 17, 2013}}</ref>

The president of Boston's City Council, [[Stephen J. Murphy]], told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.washingtonpost.com/world/national-security/security-video-may-show-boston-marathon-bomb-suspect-report-of-arrest-premature/2013/04/17/2be1a3f6-a78b-11e2-b029-8fb7e977ef71_story.html|title= Security video may show Boston Marathon bomb suspect; report of arrest premature |author = David Montgomery |author2 = Marc Fisher|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=April 17, 2013|accessdate=April 18, 2013}}</ref> Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.<ref>{{cite news|title=Videos Said to Show Clear Images of 2 Bombing Suspects|url=http://www.nytimes.com/2013/04/19/us/boston-set-to-mourn-bombing-victims.html?hp&_r=0|accessdate=April 18, 2013|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=April 18, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Authorities have clear video images of two suspects|url=http://bostonglobe.com/metro/2013/04/18/authorities-have-clear-video-images-two-suspects/YejgNWAcmChcx2lUXigs5I/story.html|accessdate=April 18, 2013|newspaper=[[The Boston Globe]]|date=April 18, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Video images yield two possible Boston bombing suspects|url=http://www.latimes.com/news/nationworld/nation/la-na-boston-bombings-investigation-20130418,0,2651203.story|accessdate=April 18, 2013|newspaper=[[The Los Angeles Times]]|date=April 18, 2013}}</ref>

===False reports of arrests===
On April 17, false reports that an arrest had been made originated on AP and CNN and were repeated in other media. The FBI issued a statement saying that there had been no arrests and cautioning news outlets not to be reckless, saying "these stories often have unintended consequences".

At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

The FBI reports that this pressure cooker fragment is part of one of the explosive devices|thumb|left
A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.

On April 17, false reports that an arrest had been made originated on AP and CNN and were repeated in other media. The FBI issued a statement saying that there had been no arrests and cautioning news outlets not to be reckless, saying "these stories often have unintended consequences".

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

The FBI reports that this pressure cooker fragment is part of one of the explosive devices|thumb|left
A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.

thumb|Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, the 19-year-old suspect currently at largeIn a news conference held at around 5:20 p.m. on April 18, the FBI released photos and a video of two suspects and sought the public's help in identifying them. According to the FBI, one of the men pictured was seen placing a backpack at the scene minutes before the second bomb exploded. Authorities identified two brothers, 26-year-old Tamerlan Tsarnaev () and 19-year-old Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev  (), as suspects. Chechens from the Russian Caucasus, the two immigrated to the United States in 2000 or 2001.  They have been living in Cambridge, Massachusetts, for the last year.

Tamerlan Tsarnaev (October 21, 1986 – April 19, 2013), who presented himself as a devout Muslim, was killed during a massive manhunt launched in the early hours of April 19.  Tamerlan Tsarnaev was born in Chechnya.   Before his death, he was quoted as saying, "I don't have a single American friend, I don't understand them."   

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev (born July 22, 1993) posted links to websites about Islam and Chechen separatism on his page on VKontakte, a Russian social networking service. On his page, he listed his languages as English, Russian and Chechen; his worldview was given as "Islam" and his personal priority was "career and money". According to his VKontakte account, he attended School No. 1 in Makhachkala, Dagestan, Russia, in 2001, and graduated from Cambridge Rindge and Latin School in 2011. Classmates and acquaintances described him as a kind, sociable individual who was well-integrated into his school community and was "very relaxed." He received a $2,500 scholarship to attend college from the city of Cambridge the year he graduated; he had also been named a wrestling all-star the same year.  At the time of the incident, he was a student at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth with a major in marine biology.

Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

The FBI reports that this pressure cooker fragment is part of one of the explosive devices|thumb|left
A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.

False reports of arrests
On April 17, false reports that an arrest had been made originated on AP and CNN and were repeated in other media. The FBI issued a statement saying that there had been no arrests and cautioning news outlets not to be reckless, saying "these stories often have unintended consequences".

Suspect photos released

The FBI has released photo and videos of 2 suspects and is seeking the public's help in identifying them.

Authorities identified two brothers, 26-year-old Tamerlan Tsarnaev () and 19-year-old Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev  (), as suspects. Chechens from the Russian Caucasus, the two immigrated to the United States in 2000 or 2001.  They have been living in Cambridge, Massachusetts, for the last year.

Tamerlan Tsarnaev (October 21, 1986 – April 19, 2013), who presented himself as a devout Muslim, was killed during a massive manhunt launched in the early hours of April 19.  Born in Chechnya,   before his death, he was quoted as saying, "I don't have a single American friend, I don't understand them."   

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev (born July 22, 1993) posted links to websites about Islam and Chechen separatism on his page on VKontakte, a Russian social networking service. On his page, he listed his languages as English, Russian and Chechen; his worldview was given as "Islam" and his personal priority was "career and money". According to his VKontakte account, he attended School No. 1 in Makhachkala, Dagestan, Russia, in 2001, and graduated from Cambridge Rindge and Latin School in 2011. Classmates and acquaintances described him as a kind, sociable individual who was well-integrated into his school community and was "very relaxed." He received a $2,500 scholarship to attend college from the city of Cambridge the year he graduated; he had also been named a wrestling all-star the same year.  At the time of the incident, he was a student at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth with a major in marine biology.

Authorities identified two brothers, 26-year-old Tamerlan Tsarnaev () and 19-year-old Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev  (), as suspects. Chechens from the Russian Caucasus, the two immigrated to the United States in 2000 or 2001.  They have been living in Cambridge, Massachusetts, for the last year.

Tamerlan Tsarnaev (October 21, 1986 – April 19, 2013), who presented himself as a devout Muslim, was killed during a massive manhunt launched in the early hours of April 19.  Tamerlan Tsarnaev was born in Chechnya.   Before his death, he was quoted as saying, "I don't have a single American friend, I don't understand them."   

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev (born July 22, 1993) posted links to websites about Islam and Chechen separatism on his page on VKontakte, a Russian social networking service. On his page, he listed his languages as English, Russian and Chechen; his worldview was given as "Islam" and his personal priority was "career and money". According to his VKontakte account, he attended School No. 1 in Makhachkala, Dagestan, Russia, in 2001, and graduated from Cambridge Rindge and Latin School in 2011. Classmates and acquaintances described him as a kind, sociable individual who was well-integrated into his school community and was "very relaxed." He received a $2,500 scholarship to attend college from the city of Cambridge the year he graduated; he had also been named a wrestling all-star the same year.  At the time of the incident, he was a student at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth with a major in marine biology.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

The FBI reports that this pressure cooker fragment is part of one of the explosive devices|thumb|left
A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.

thumb|Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, the 19-year-old suspect currently at largeIn a news conference held at around 5:20 p.m. on April 18, the FBI released photos and a video of two suspects and sought the public's help in identifying them. According to the FBI, one of the men pictured was seen placing a backpack at the scene minutes before the second bomb exploded. Authorities identified two brothers, 26-year-old Tamerlan Tsarnaev () and 19-year-old Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev  (), as suspects. Chechens from the Russian Caucasus, the two immigrated to the United States in 2000 or 2001.  They have been living in Cambridge, Massachusetts, for the last year.

Tamerlan Tsarnaev (October 21, 1986 – April 19, 2013), who presented himself as a devout Muslim, was killed during a massive manhunt launched in the early hours of April 19.  Tamerlan Tsarnaev was born in Chechnya.  Before his death, he was quoted as saying, "I don't have a single American friend, I don't understand them."  The older Tsarnaev was arrested in 2009 for domestic assault and battery after assaulting his girlfriend.  NBC News has stated that Tamerlan Tsarnaev became a United States citizen on September 11, 2012.  

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev (born July 22, 1993) posted links to websites about Islam and Chechen separatism on his page on VKontakte, a Russian social networking service. On his page, he listed his languages as English, Russian and Chechen; his worldview was given as "Islam" and his personal priority was "career and money". According to his VKontakte account, he attended School No. 1 in Makhachkala, Dagestan, Russia, in 2001, and graduated from Cambridge Rindge and Latin School in 2011. Classmates and acquaintances described him as a kind, sociable individual who was well-integrated into his school community and was "very relaxed." He received a $2,500 scholarship to attend college from the city of Cambridge the year he graduated; he had also been named a wrestling all-star the same year.  At the time of the incident, he was a student at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth with a major in marine biology.

thumb|Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, the 19-year-old suspect currently at largeIn a news conference held at around 5:20 p.m. on April 18, the FBI released photos and a video of two suspects and sought the public's help in identifying them. According to the FBI, one of the men pictured was seen placing a backpack at the scene minutes before the second bomb exploded. Authorities identified two brothers, 26-year-old Tamerlan Tsarnaev (Chechen language: Тамерлан Царнаев) and 19-year-old Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev  (Chechen language: Джохар Царнаев), as suspects. Chechens from the Russian Caucasus, the two immigrated to the United States in 2000 or 2001.  They have been living in Cambridge, Massachusetts, for the last year.

Tamerlan Tsarnaev (October 21, 1986 – April 19, 2013), who presented himself as a devout Muslim according to his family, was killed during a massive manhunt launched in the early hours of April 19.  Tamerlan Tsarnaev was born in Chechnya.  Before his death, he was quoted as saying, "I don't have a single American friend, I don't understand them."  The older Tsarnaev was arrested in 2009 for domestic assault and battery after assaulting his girlfriend.  NBC News has stated that Tamerlan Tsarnaev became a United States citizen on September 11, 2012.  

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev (born July 22, 1993) posted links to websites about Islam and Chechen separatism on his page on VKontakte, a Russian social networking service. On his page, he listed his languages as English, Russian and Chechen; his worldview was given as "Islam" and his personal priority was "career and money". According to his VKontakte account, he attended School No. 1 in Makhachkala, Dagestan, Russia, in 2001, and graduated from Cambridge Rindge and Latin School in 2011. Classmates and acquaintances described him as a kind, sociable individual who was well-integrated into his school community and was "very relaxed." He received a $2,500 scholarship to attend college from the city of Cambridge the year he graduated; he had also been named a wrestling all-star the same year.  At the time of the incident, he was a student at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth with a major in marine biology.

[[File:FBI and JTTF at Boston bombing.jpg|thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media]]

morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of [[Revere, Massachusetts |Revere]], the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest".<ref name="Fox News1"/><ref>{{cite news|title=Large police presence in Revere connected to Boston bombing|url= http://www.myfoxboston.com/story/21986273/large-police-presence-in-revere-connected-to-boston-bombing |publisher=[[WFXT]]|accessdate=April 16, 2013}}</ref> CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."<ref name="CNN_FBI">{{cite web|title=FBI will try to rebuild Boston United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative [[Peter T. King|Peter King]], member of the [[United States House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence|House Intelligence Committee]] said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."<ref>{{cite web|title=Live updates: Obama calls Boston bombings a 'heinous, cowardly' act of terror |url= http://www.latimes.com/news/nation/nationnow/la-na-nn-boston-searches-for-clues-to-bombing-that-killed-3-injured-176-20130416,0,318317.story?page=2 |work=LA Times|accessdate=April 16, 2013}}</ref>

[[File:Pressure cooker bomb.jpg|The FBI reports that this pressure cooker fragment is part of one of the explosive devices|thumb|left]]
A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a [[pressure cooker]] packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a [[backpack]].<ref name="CNN_FBI"/> The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop.<ref>{{cite news|last=Ellement|first=John|title=Boston Medical Center reports five-year-old boy in critical condition, 23 victims treated from Boston Marathon bombings|url=http://www.boston.com/metrodesk/2013/04/17/boston-medical-center-reports-five-year-old-boy-critical-condition-victims-treated-from-boston-marathon-bombings/gkKXBTqL2jyNhsC2Kz5GyO/story.html|accessdate=April 17, 2013|newspaper=The Boston Globe|date=April 17, 2013|author2=Brian Ballou}}</ref> Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb.<ref>{{cite news|url= http://www.cbsnews.com/8301-201_162-57579766/boston-marathon-bombings-suburban-apartment-searched/ |title=FBI seeks images in Boston Marathon bomb probe; new details emerge on explosives |work =CBS News|date=April 16, 2013|accessdate=April 16, 2013}}</ref> Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.<ref name="Lister">{{cite web|url=http://edition.cnn.com/2013/04/16/us/boston-marathon-lone-wolf/|title=Boston Marathon bombs similar to 'lone wolf' devices, experts say|last=Lister|first=Tim|coauthors=Paul Cruickshank|date=April 17, 2013|work=[[CNN]]|accessdate=April 17, 2013}}</ref>

The president of Boston's City Council, [[Stephen J. Murphy]], told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.washingtonpost.com/world/national-security/security-video-may-show-boston-marathon-bomb-suspect-report-of-arrest-premature/2013/04/17/2be1a3f6-a78b-11e2-b029-8fb7e977ef71_story.html|title= Security video may show Boston Marathon bomb suspect; report of arrest premature |author = David Montgomery |author2 = Marc Fisher|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=April 17, 2013|accessdate=April 18, 2013}}</ref> Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.<ref>{{cite news|title=Videos Said to Show Clear Images of 2 Bombing Suspects|url=http://www.nytimes.com/2013/04/19/us/boston-set-to-mourn-bombing-victims.html?hp&_r=0|accessdate=April 18, 2013|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=April 18, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Authorities have clear video images of two suspects|url=http://bostonglobe.com/metro/2013/04/18/authorities-have-clear-video-images-two-suspects/YejgNWAcmChcx2lUXigs5I/story.html|accessdate=April 18, 2013|newspaper=[[The Boston Globe]]|date=April 18, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Video images yield two possible Boston bombing suspects|url=http://www.latimes.com/news/nationworld/nation/la-na-boston-bombings-investigation-20130418,0,2651203.story|accessdate=April 18, 2013|newspaper=[[The Los Angeles Times]]|date=April 18, 2013}}</ref>

On April 17, false reports that an arrest had been made originated on AP and CNN and were repeated in other media. The FBI issued a statement saying that there had been no arrests and cautioning news outlets not to be reckless, saying "these stories often have unintended consequences".

Tamerlan Tsarnaev (October 21, 1986 – April 19, 2013) was killed during a massive manhunt launched in the early hours of April 19.  Tamerlan Tsarnaev was born in Chechnya.  Before his death, he was quoted as saying, "I don't have a single American friend, I don't understand them."  The older Tsarnaev was arrested in 2009 for domestic assault and battery after assaulting his girlfriend.  NBC News has stated that Tamerlan Tsarnaev became a United States citizen on September 11, 2012.  

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev (born July 22, 1993) posted links to websites about Islam and Chechen separatism on his page on VKontakte, a Russian social networking service. On his page, he listed his languages as English, Russian and Chechen; his worldview was given as "Islam" and his personal priority was "career and money". According to his VKontakte account, he attended School No. 1 in Makhachkala, Dagestan, Russia, in 2001, and graduated from Cambridge Rindge and Latin School in 2011. Classmates and acquaintances described him as a kind, sociable individual who was well-integrated into his school community and was "very relaxed." He received a $2,500 scholarship to attend college from the city of Cambridge the year he graduated; he had also been named a wrestling all-star the same year.  At the time of the incident, he was a student at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth with a major in marine biology.

Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.
