The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

The FBI reports that this pressure cooker fragment is part of one of the explosive devices|thumb|left
A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.

In a news conference held at around 5:20 p.m. on April 18, the FBI released photos and a video of two suspects and sought the public's help in identifying them. According to the FBI, one of the men pictured was seen placing a backpack at the scene minutes before the second bomb exploded. Authorities identified two brothers, 26-year-old Tamerlan Tsarnaev (Chechen language: Тамерлан Царнаев) and 19-year-old Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev (Chechen language: Джохар Царнаев), as suspects.  Ethnic Chechens from the North Caucasus, the two immigrated to the United States in 2000 or 2001.  They have been living in Cambridge, Massachusetts, for the last year.  Both brothers are Muslim.

Tamerlan Tsarnaev (October 21, 1986 – April 19, 2013) was killed during a massive manhunt launched in the early hours of April 19. He was quoted as previously saying, "I don't have a single American friend, I don't understand them."  The older Tsarnaev was arrested in 2009 for domestic assault and battery after assaulting his girlfriend.  Tamerlan Tsarnaev was not a U.S. citizen but was a permanent resident.  

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev (born July 22, 1993), at the time of the incident, was a student at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth with a major in marine biology.  He became a naturalized U.S. citizen on September 11, 2012.  On television, his uncle pleaded with Dzhokhar to turn himself in.

thumb|150px|Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, the 19-year-old suspect currently at large

In a news conference held at around 5:20 p.m. on April 18, the FBI released photos and a video of two suspects and sought the public's help in identifying them. According to the FBI, one of the men pictured was seen placing a backpack at the scene minutes before the second bomb exploded. Authorities identified two brothers, 26-year-old Tamerlan Tsarnaev (Chechen language: Тамерлан Царнаев) and 19-year-old Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev (Chechen language: Джохар Царнаев), as suspects.  Ethnic Chechens from the North Caucasus, the two immigrated to the United States in 2000 or 2001.  They have been living in Cambridge, Massachusetts, for the last ten years.  They had previously lived in Makhachkala, Dagestan, Russia.   Both brothers are Muslim.

Tamerlan Tsarnaev (October 21, 1986 – April 19, 2013) was killed during a massive manhunt launched in the early hours of April 19. He was quoted as previously saying, "I don't have a single American friend, I don't understand them."  The older Tsarnaev was arrested in 2009 for domestic assault and battery after assaulting his girlfriend.  Tamerlan Tsarnaev was not a U.S. citizen but was a permanent resident.  

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev (born July 22, 1993), at the time of the incident, was a student at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth with a major in marine biology.  He became a naturalized U.S. citizen on September 11, 2012.  On television, his uncle pleaded with Dzhokhar to turn himself in.

At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.

thumb|right|upright|Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, the 19-year-old suspect currently at large

In a 5:20 p.m. news conference on April 18, the FBI released photos and a video of two suspects, and sought the public's help in identifying them. According to the FBI, one of the suspects was seen placing a backpack at the scene minutes before the second bomb exploded. 

Authorities identified two brothers, 26-year-old Tamerlan Tsarnaev (Chechen language: Тамерлан Царнаев) and 19-year-old Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev (Chechen language: Джохар Царнаев), as the suspects. Ethnic Chechens from the North Caucasus, the two immigrated to the United States in 2002.  They had been living in Cambridge, Massachusetts, for the last ten years.  They had previously lived in Makhachkala, Dagestan, Russia.  Both brothers are Muslims.

Tamerlan Tsarnaev (October 21, 1986 – April 19, 2013) was killed during a massive manhunt launched in the early hours of April 19. He had been quoted as saying, "I don't have a single American friend, I don't understand them."  He had been arrested in 2009 for domestic assault and battery after assaulting his girlfriend.  Tamerlan Tsarnaev was not a U.S. citizen but was a permanent resident.  

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev (born July 22, 1993), at the time of the incident, was a student at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth with a major in marine biology.  He became a naturalized U.S. citizen on September 11, 2012.  On television, his uncle pleaded with Dzhokhar to turn himself in.

Investigation.wikitext:
[[File:Hazmat biohazard team at Boston Marathon near the finish line 07.jpeg|thumb|[[Dangerous goods|Hazmat]] workers near the scene]]

The [[Federal Bureau of Investigation]], which is investigating the attack along with the [[Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives]] (ATF), the [[Central Intelligence Agency]], and the [[National Counterterrorism Center]],<ref name= "Hosenball">{{cite web| url= http://www.globalpost.com/dispatch/news/thomson-reuters/130415/investigators-scour-video-photos-boston-marathon-bomb-clues |title= Investigators scour video, photos for Boston Marathon bomb clues|last1= Hosenball| first1=Mark |first2= Svea| last2=Herbst-Bayliss |date=April 16, 2013|work= [[GlobalPost]]|publisher= [[Thomson Reuters]] |accessdate =April 16, 2013}}</ref> is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.<ref name="Fox News1"/>

[[File:FBI and JTTF at Boston bombing.jpg|thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media]]
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner [[Edward F. Davis]] told reporters that no suspect was in custody.<ref name="Hunter">{{cite web|url=http://livewire.talkingpointsmemo.com/entry/boston-police-commissioner-there-is-no-suspect-in|title=Boston attacks|url=http://www.cbsnews.com/8301-201_162-57579893/sources-injured-saudi-man-not-a-suspect-in-boston-attacks/|last=Sison |first=Bree|publisher=CBS News|accessdate=April 17, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Nelson|first=Steven|title=Boston Police: 'We Are Questioning Many People'|url=http://www.usnews.com/news/newsgram/articles/2013/04/15/boston-police-we-are-questioning-many-people |accessdate=April 16, 2013|newspaper=[[U.S. News & World Report]]}}</ref> Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of [[Revere, Massachusetts |Revere]], the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest".<ref name="Fox News1"/><ref>{{cite news|title=Large police presence in Revere connected to Boston bombing|url= http://www.myfoxboston.com/story/21986273/large-police-presence-in-revere-connected-to-boston-bombing |publisher=[[WFXT]]|accessdate=April 16, 2013}}</ref> CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."<ref name="CNN_FBI">{{cite web|title=FBI will try to rebuild Boston bombs|url=http://www.cnn.com/2013/04/15/us/boston-marathon-investigation/index.html|last=Smith |first=Matt|coauthors=Josh Levs|publisher=CNN|accessdate=April 17, 2013}}</ref>

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative [[Peter T. King|Peter King]], member of the [[United States House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence|House Intelligence Committee]] said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."<ref>{{cite web|title=Live updates: Obama calls Boston bombings a 'heinous, cowardly' act of terror |url= http://www.latimes.com/news/nation/nationnow/la-na-nn-boston-searches-for-clues-to-bombing-that-killed-3-injured-176-20130416,0,318317.story?page=2 |work=LA Times|accessdate=April 16, 2013}}</ref>

[[File:Pressure cooker bomb.jpg|The FBI reports that this pressure cooker fragment is part of one of the explosive devices|thumb|left]]
A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a [[pressure cooker]] packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a [[backpack]].<ref name="CNN_FBI"/> The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop.<ref>{{cite news|last=Ellement|first=John|title=Boston Medical Center reports five-year-old boy in critical condition, 23 victims treated from Boston Marathon bombings|url=http://www.boston.com/metrodesk/2013/04/17/boston-medical-center-reports-five-year-old-boy-critical-condition-victims-treated-from-boston-marathon-bombings/gkKXBTqL2jyNhsC2Kz5GyO/story.html|accessdate=April 17, 2013|newspaper=The Boston Globe|date=April 17, 2013|author2=Brian Ballou}}</ref> Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb.<ref>{{cite news|url= http://www.cbsnews.com/8301-201_162-57579766/boston-marathon-bombings-suburban-apartment-searched/ |title=FBI seeks images in Boston Marathon bomb probe; new details emerge on explosives |work =CBS News|date=April 16, 2013|accessdate=April 16, 2013}}</ref> Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.<ref name="Lister">{{cite web|url=http://edition.cnn.com/2013/04/16/us/boston-marathon-lone-wolf/|title=Boston Marathon bombs similar to 'lone wolf' devices, experts say|last=Lister|first=Tim|coauthors=Paul Cruickshank|date=April 17, 2013|work=[[CNN]]|accessdate=April 17, 2013}}</ref>

The president of Boston's City Council, [[Stephen J. Murphy]], told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.washingtonpost.com/world/national-security/security-video-may-show-boston-marathon-bomb-suspect-report-of-arrest-premature/2013/04/17/2be1a3f6-a78b-11e2-b029-8fb7e977ef71_story.html|title= Security video may show Boston Marathon bomb suspect; report of arrest premature |author = David Montgomery |author2 = Marc Fisher|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=April 17, 2013|accessdate=April 18, 2013}}</ref> Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.<ref>{{cite news|title=Videos Said to Show Clear Images of 2 Bombing Suspects|url=http://www.nytimes.com/2013/04/19/us/boston-set-to-mourn-bombing-victims.html?hp&_r=0|accessdate=April 18, 2013|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=April 18, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Authorities have clear video images of two suspects|url=http://bostonglobe.com/metro/2013/04/18/authorities-have-clear-video-images-two-suspects/YejgNWAcmChcx2lUXigs5I/story.html|accessdate=April 18, 2013|newspaper=[[The Boston Globe]]|date=April 18, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Video images yield two possible Boston bombing suspects|url=http://www.latimes.com/news/nationworld/nation/la-na-boston-bombings-investigation-20130418,0,2651203.story|accessdate=April 18, 2013|newspaper=[[The Los Angeles Times]]|date=April 18, 2013}}</ref>

===False reports of arrests===
On April 17, false reports that an arrest had been made originated on AP and CNN and were repeated in other media. The FBI issued a statement saying that there had been no arrests and cautioning news outlets not to be reckless, saying "these stories often have unintended consequences".

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

The FBI reports that this pressure cooker fragment is part of one of the explosive devices|thumb|left
A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.

False reports of arrests
On April 17, false reports that an arrest had been made originated on AP and CNN and were repeated in other media. The FBI issued a statement saying that there had been no arrests and cautioning news outlets not to be reckless, saying "these stories often have unintended consequences".

The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.

Suspects.plaintext:
thumb|right|150px|upright|Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, the 19-year-old suspect currently at large

In a 5:20 p.m. news conference on April 18, the FBI released photos and a video of two suspects, and sought the public's help in identifying them. According to the FBI, one of the suspects was seen placing a backpack at the scene minutes before the second bomb exploded. 

Authorities identified two brothers as the suspects: 26-year-old Tamerlan Tsarnaev (Chechen language: Тамерлан Царнаев) and 19-year-old Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev (Chechen language: Джохар Царнаев). Ethnic Chechens from the North Caucasus, born in Kyrgyzstan, the two immigrated to the United States in 2002.  They had been living in Cambridge, Massachusetts, for the prior ten years.  They had previously lived in Tokmok, Kyrgyzstan and Makhachkala, Dagestan, Russia.  Both brothers are Muslims.

Tamerlan Tsarnaev (October 21, 1986 – April 19, 2013) was killed during a massive manhunt launched in the early hours of April 19. He had been quoted as saying, "I don't have a single American friend, I don't understand them."  He had been arrested in 2009 for domestic assault and battery, after assaulting his girlfriend.  He was not a U.S. citizen, but was a permanent resident.  

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev (born July 22, 1993) at the time of the incident was a student at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth, with a major in marine biology.  He became a naturalized U.S. citizen on September 11, 2012.  On television, his uncle pleaded with Dzhokhar to turn himself in.

Although the brothers' uncle and aunt insisted that Islam played no role in their actions, several analysts suspect that they were influenced by Islamic jihad (and not the Chechen insurgent cause). The suspects' YouTube, Twitter, and other accounts reportedly have several Islamic references. One suspect reportedly published a video of Osama bin Laden calling on Muslims to kill Americans, Christians, and Jews.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

The FBI reports that this pressure cooker fragment is part of one of the explosive devices|thumb|left
A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.

False reports of arrests
On April 17, false reports that an arrest had been made originated on AP and CNN and were repeated in other media. The FBI issued a statement saying that there had been no arrests and cautioning news outlets not to be reckless, saying "these stories often have unintended consequences".

Suspect photos released

The FBI has released photo and videos of 2 suspects and is seeking the public's help in identifying them.

Suspects.plaintext:
thumb|right|150px|upright|Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, the 19-year-old suspect currently at large

In a 5:20 p.m. news conference on April 18, the FBI released photos and a video of two suspects, and sought the public's help in identifying them. According to the FBI, one of the suspects was seen placing a backpack at the scene minutes before the second bomb exploded. 

Authorities identified two brothers as the suspects: 26-year-old Tamerlan Tsarnaev (Chechen language: Тамерлан Царнаев) and 19-year-old Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev (Chechen language: Джохар Царнаев). Ethnic Chechens from the North Caucasus, the two immigrated to the United States in 2002.  They had been living in Cambridge, Massachusetts, for the prior ten years.  They had previously lived in Tokmok, Kyrgyzstan and Makhachkala, Dagestan, Russia.  Both brothers are Muslims.

Tamerlan Tsarnaev (October 21, 1986 – April 19, 2013) was killed during a massive manhunt launched in the early hours of April 19. He had been quoted as saying, "I don't have a single American friend, I don't understand them."  He had been arrested in 2009 for domestic assault and battery, after assaulting his girlfriend.  He was not a U.S. citizen, but was a permanent resident. He was born in Russia. 

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev (born July 22, 1993) at the time of the incident was a student at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth, with a major in marine biology.  He was born in Kyrgyzstan.  He became a naturalized U.S. citizen on September 11, 2012.  On television, his uncle pleaded with Dzhokhar to turn himself in.

The brothers' uncle and aunt insisted that Islam played no role in their motivation for the bombing.

Suspects.plaintext:
thumb|right|150px|upright|Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, the 19-year-old suspect currently at large

In a 5:20 p.m. news conference on April 18, the FBI released photos and a video of two suspects, and sought the public's help in identifying them. According to the FBI, one of the suspects was seen placing a backpack at the scene minutes before the second bomb exploded. 

Authorities identified two brothers as the suspects: 26-year-old Tamerlan Tsarnaev and 19-year-old Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev. Ethnic Chechens from the North Caucasus, the two immigrated to the United States in 2002.  They had been living in Cambridge, Massachusetts, for the prior ten years.  They had previously lived in Tokmok, Kyrgyzstan and Makhachkala, Dagestan, Russia.  Both brothers are Muslims. The brothers' uncle and aunt insisted that the religion  played no role in their motivation for the bombing.

Tamerlan Tsarnaev (October 21, 1986 – April 19, 2013) was killed during a massive manhunt launched in the early hours of April 19. He had been quoted as saying, "I don't have a single American friend, I don't understand them."  He had been arrested in 2009 for domestic assault and battery, after assaulting his girlfriend.  He was not a U.S. citizen, but was a permanent resident. He was born in Russia. 

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev (born July 22, 1993) at the time of the incident was a student at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth, with a major in marine biology.  He was born in Kyrgyzstan.  He became a naturalized U.S. citizen on September 11, 2012.  On television, his uncle pleaded with Dzhokhar to turn himself in.

In a 5:20 p.m. news conference on April 18, the FBI released photos and a video of two suspects, and sought the public's help in identifying them. According to the FBI, one of the suspects was seen placing a backpack at the scene minutes before the second bomb exploded. 

Authorities identified two brothers as the suspects: 26-year-old Tamerlan Tsarnaev and 19-year-old Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev. Ethnic Chechens from the North Caucasus, the two immigrated to the United States in 2002.  They had been living in Cambridge, Massachusetts, for the prior ten years.  They had previously lived in Tokmok, Kyrgyzstan and Makhachkala, Dagestan, Russia.  Both brothers are Muslims. The brothers' uncle and aunt insisted that the religion  played no role in their motivation for the bombing.

Tamerlan Tsarnaev (October 21, 1986 – April 19, 2013) was killed during a massive manhunt launched in the early hours of April 19. He had been quoted as saying, "I don't have a single American friend, I don't understand them."  He had been arrested in 2009 for domestic assault and battery, after assaulting his girlfriend.  He was not a U.S. citizen, but was a permanent resident. He was born in Russia. 

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev (born July 22, 1993) at the time of the incident was a student at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth, with a major in marine biology.  He was born in Kyrgyzstan.  He became a naturalized U.S. citizen on September 11, 2012.  On television, his uncle pleaded with Dzhokhar to turn himself in.

The suspect Tsnaraev was taken into custody alive.

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev (born July 22, 1993) at the time of the incident was a student at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth, with a major in marine biology.  He was born in Kyrgyzstan.  He became a naturalized U.S. citizen on September 11, 2012.  On television, his uncle pleaded with Dzhokhar to turn himself in.

The suspect Tsnaraev, after a long stand-off on the boat, was taken into custody alive.

In a 5:20 p.m. news conference on April 18, the FBI released photos and a video of two suspects, and sought the public's help in identifying them. According to the FBI, one of the suspects was seen placing a backpack at the scene minutes before the second bomb exploded. 

Authorities identified two brothers as the suspects: 26-year-old Tamerlan Tsarnaev and 19-year-old Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev. Ethnic Chechens from the North Caucasus, the two immigrated to the United States in 2002.  They had been living in Cambridge, Massachusetts, for the prior ten years.  They had previously lived in Tokmok, Kyrgyzstan and Makhachkala, Dagestan, Russia.  Both brothers are Muslims. The brothers' uncle and aunt insisted that the religion  played no role in their motivation for the bombing.

Tamerlan Tsarnaev (October 21, 1986 – April 19, 2013) was killed during a massive manhunt launched in the early hours of April 19. He had been quoted as saying, "I don't have a single American friend, I don't understand them."  He had been arrested in 2009 for domestic assault and battery, after assaulting his girlfriend.  He was not a U.S. citizen, but was a permanent resident. He was born in Russia. 

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev (born July 22, 1993) at the time of the incident was a student at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth, with a major in marine biology.  He was born in Kyrgyzstan.  He became a naturalized U.S. citizen on September 11, 2012.  On television, his uncle pleaded with Dzhokhar to turn himself in.

In the evening of April 19, authorities surrounded Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev as he took refuge hiding under the canvas of a boat in the backyard of a property at 67 Franklin St. in Watertown. He was taken into custody after a standoff.

thumb|right|150px|upright|Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, the younger of the two brothers

In a 5:20 p.m. news conference on April 18, the FBI released photos and a video of two suspects, and sought the public's help in identifying them. According to the FBI, one of the suspects was seen placing a backpack at the scene minutes before the second bomb exploded. 

Authorities identified two brothers as the suspects: 26-year-old Tamerlan Tsarnaev and 19-year-old Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev. Ethnic Chechens from the North Caucasus, the two immigrated to the United States in 2002.  They had been living in Cambridge, Massachusetts, for the prior ten years.  They had previously lived in Tokmok, Kyrgyzstan and Makhachkala, Dagestan, Russia.  Both brothers are Muslims. The brothers' uncle and aunt insisted that the religion  played no role in their motivation for the bombing.

Tamerlan Tsarnaev (October 21, 1986 – April 19, 2013) was killed during a massive manhunt launched in the early hours of April 19. He had been quoted as saying, "I don't have a single American friend, I don't understand them."  He had been arrested in 2009 for domestic assault and battery, after assaulting his girlfriend.  He was not a U.S. citizen, but was a permanent resident. He was born in Russia. 

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev (born July 22, 1993) at the time of the incident was a student at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth, with a major in marine biology.  He was born in Kyrgyzstan.  He became a naturalized U.S. citizen on September 11, 2012.  On television, his uncle pleaded with Dzhokhar to turn himself in.

In the evening of April 19, authorities surrounded Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev as he took refuge hiding under the canvas of a boat in the backyard of a property at 67 Franklin St. in Watertown. He was taken into federal custody after a standoff.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

The FBI reports that this pressure cooker fragment is part of one of the explosive devices|thumb|left
A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.

In a 5:20 p.m. news conference on April 18, the FBI released photos and a video of two suspects, and sought the public's help in identifying them. According to the FBI, one of the suspects was seen placing a backpack at the scene minutes before the second bomb exploded. 

Authorities identified two brothers as the suspects: 26-year-old Tamerlan Tsarnaev and 19-year-old Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev. Ethnic Chechens from the North Caucasus, the two immigrated to the United States in 2002.  They had been living in Cambridge, Massachusetts, for the prior ten years.  They had previously lived in Tokmok, Kyrgyzstan and Makhachkala, Dagestan, Russia.  Both brothers are Muslims. The brothers' uncle and aunt insisted that the religion  played no role in their motivation for the bombing.

Tamerlan Tsarnaev (October 21, 1986 – April 19, 2013) was killed during a massive manhunt launched in the early hours of April 19. He had been quoted as saying, "I don't have a single American friend, I don't understand them."  He had been arrested in 2009 for domestic assault and battery, after assaulting his girlfriend.  He was not a U.S. citizen, but was a permanent resident. He was born in Russia. 

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev (born July 22, 1993) at the time of the incident was a student at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth, with a major in marine biology.  He was born in Kyrgyzstan.  He became a naturalized U.S. citizen on September 11, 2012.  On television, his uncle pleaded with Dzhokhar to turn himself in.

In the evening of April 19, authorities surrounded Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev as he took refuge hiding under the canvas of a boat in the backyard of a property at 67 Franklin St. in Watertown. He was taken into federal custody after a standoff.

Suspects.plaintext:
thumb|right|150px|upright|Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, the younger of the two brothers

In a 5:20 p.m. news conference on April 18, the FBI released photos and a video of two suspects, and sought the public's help in identifying them. According to the FBI, one of the suspects was seen placing a backpack at the scene minutes before the second bomb exploded. 

Authorities identified two brothers as the suspects: 26-year-old Tamerlan Tsarnaev and 19-year-old Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev. Ethnic Chechens from the North Caucasus, the two immigrated to the United States in 2002.  They had been living in Cambridge, Massachusetts, for the prior ten years.  They had previously lived in Tokmok, Kyrgyzstan and Makhachkala, Dagestan, Russia.  Both brothers are Muslims. The brothers' uncle and aunt insisted that the religion  played no role in their motivation for the bombing.

Tamerlan Tsarnaev (October 21, 1986 – April 19, 2013) was killed during a massive manhunt launched in the early hours of April 19. He had been quoted as saying, "I don't have a single American friend, I don't understand them."  He had been arrested in 2009 for domestic assault and battery, after assaulting his girlfriend.  He was not a U.S. citizen, but was a permanent resident. He was born in Russia. 

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev (born July 22, 1993) at the time of the incident was a student at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth, with a major in marine biology.  He was born in Kyrgyzstan.  He became a naturalized U.S. citizen on September 11, 2012.  On television, his uncle pleaded with Dzhokhar to turn himself in. Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev was taken into federal custody after a standoff.

Arrest.wikitext: In the evening of April 19, authorities surrounded Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev as he took refuge hiding under the canvas of a boat in the backyard of a property at 67 Franklin St. in Watertown. He was taken into custody after a standoff.<ref>{{cite web|title=Bombing suspect surrounded in Watertown|url=http://www.lowellsun.com/breakingnews/ci_23065406/sun-staff-and-news-services|publisher=The Lowell Sun|accessdate=April 20, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Shots Fired In Watertown (UPDATE: Police Have Suspect In Custody)|url=http://www.mediaite.com/online/breaking-shots-fired-in-watertown/|publisher=Mediaite|accessdate=20 April 2013}}</ref>

The [[Federal Bureau of Investigation]], which is investigating the attack along with the [[Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives]] (ATF), the [[Central Intelligence Agency]], and the [[National Counterterrorism Center]],<ref name= "Hosenball">{{cite web| url= http://www.globalpost.com/dispatch/news/thomson-reuters/130415/investigators-scour-video-photos-boston-marathon-bomb-clues |title= Investigators scour video, photos for Boston Marathon bomb clues|last1= Hosenball| first1=Mark |first2= Svea| last2=Herbst-Bayliss |date=April 16, 2013|work= [[GlobalPost]]|publisher= [[Thomson Reuters]] |accessdate =April 16, 2013}}</ref> is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.<ref name="Fox News1"/>

[[File:FBI and JTTF at Boston bombing.jpg|thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media]]
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner [[Edward F. Davis]] told reporters that no suspect was in custody.<ref name="Hunter">{{cite web|url=http://livewire.talkingpointsmemo.com/entry/boston-police-commissioner-there-is-no-suspect-in|title=Boston Police Commissioner: 'There Is No Suspect In Custody'|last=Hunter|first=Walker|date=April 16, 2013|publisher=[[Talking Points Memo]]|accessdate=April 16, 2013}}</ref> Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into [[Police custody|custody]] and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable".<ref>{{cite web|title=Injured Saudi man not a suspect in Boston attacks|url=http://www.cbsnews.com/8301-201_162-57579893/sources-injured-saudi-man-not-a-suspect-in-boston-attacks/|last=Sison |first=Bree|publisher=CBS News|accessdate=April 17, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Nelson|first=Steven|title=Boston Police: 'We Are Questioning Many People'|url=http://www.usnews.com/news/newsgram/articles/2013/04/15/boston-police-we-are-questioning-many-people |accessdate=April 16, 2013|newspaper=[[U.S. News & World Report]]}}</ref> Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of [[Revere, Massachusetts |Revere]], the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest".<ref name="Fox News1"/><ref>{{cite news|title=Large police presence in Revere connected to Boston bombing|url= http://www.myfoxboston.com/story/21986273/large-police-presence-in-revere-connected-to-boston-bombing |publisher=[[WFXT]]|accessdate=April 16, 2013}}</ref> CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."<ref name="CNN_FBI">{{cite web|title=FBI will try to rebuild Boston bombs|url=http://www.cnn.com/2013/04/15/us/boston-marathon-investigation/index.html|last=Smith |first=Matt|coauthors=Josh Levs|publisher=CNN|accessdate=April 17, 2013}}</ref>

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative [[Peter T. King|Peter King]], member of the [[United States House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence|House Intelligence Committee]] said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."<ref>{{cite web|title=Live updates: Obama calls Boston bombings a 'heinous, cowardly' act of terror |url= http://www.latimes.com/news/nation/nationnow/la-na-nn-boston-searches-for-clues-to-bombing-that-killed-3-injured-176-20130416,0,318317.story?page=2 |work=LA Times|accessdate=April 16, 2013}}</ref>

[[File:Pressure cooker bomb.jpg|The FBI reports that this pressure cooker fragment is part of one of the explosive devices|thumb|left]]
A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a [[pressure cooker]] packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a [[backpack]].<ref name="CNN_FBI"/> The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop.<ref>{{cite news|last=Ellement|first=John|title=Boston Medical Center reports five-year-old boy in critical condition, 23 victims treated from Boston Marathon bombings|url=http://www.boston.com/metrodesk/2013/04/17/boston-medical-center-reports-five-year-old-boy-critical-condition-victims-treated-from-boston-marathon-bombings/gkKXBTqL2jyNhsC2Kz5GyO/story.html|accessdate=April 17, 2013|newspaper=The Boston Globe|date=April 17, 2013|author2=Brian Ballou}}</ref> Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb.<ref>{{cite news|url= http://www.cbsnews.com/8301-201_162-57579766/boston-marathon-bombings-suburban-apartment-searched/ |title=FBI seeks images in Boston Marathon bomb probe; new details emerge on explosives |work =CBS News|date=April 16, 2013|accessdate=April 16, 2013}}</ref> Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.<ref name="Lister">{{cite web|url=http://edition.cnn.com/2013/04/16/us/boston-marathon-lone-wolf/|title=Boston Marathon bombs similar to 'lone wolf' devices, experts say|last=Lister|first=Tim|coauthors=Paul Cruickshank|date=April 17, 2013|work=[[CNN]]|accessdate=April 17, 2013}}</ref>

The president of Boston's City Council, [[Stephen J. Murphy]], told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.washingtonpost.com/world/national-security/security-video-may-show-boston-marathon-bomb-suspect-report-of-arrest-premature/2013/04/17/2be1a3f6-a78b-11e2-b029-8fb7e977ef71_story.html|title= Security video may show Boston Marathon bomb suspect; report of arrest premature |author = David Montgomery |author2 = Marc Fisher|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=April 17, 2013|accessdate=April 18, 2013}}</ref> Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.<ref>{{cite news|title=Videos Said to Show Clear Images of 2 Bombing Suspects|url=http://www.nytimes.com/2013/04/19/us/boston-set-to-mourn-bombing-victims.html?hp&_r=0|accessdate=April 18, 2013|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=April 18, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Authorities have clear video images of two suspects|url=http://bostonglobe.com/metro/2013/04/18/authorities-have-clear-video-images-two-suspects/YejgNWAcmChcx2lUXigs5I/story.html|accessdate=April 18, 2013|newspaper=[[The Boston Globe]]|date=April 18, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Video images yield two possible Boston bombing suspects|url=http://www.latimes.com/news/nationworld/nation/la-na-boston-bombings-investigation-20130418,0,2651203.story|accessdate=April 18, 2013|newspaper=[[The Los Angeles Times]]|date=April 18, 2013}}</ref>

===False reports of arrests===
On April 17, false reports that an arrest had been made originated on AP and CNN and were repeated in other media. The FBI issued a statement saying that there had been no arrests and cautioning news outlets not to be reckless, saying "these stories often have unintended consequences".

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

The FBI reports that this pressure cooker fragment is part of one of the explosive devices|thumb|left
A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.

False reports of arrests
On April 17, false reports that an arrest had been made originated on AP and CNN and were repeated in other media. The FBI issued a statement saying that there had been no arrests and cautioning news outlets not to be reckless, saying "these stories often have unintended consequences".

Suspect photos released

The FBI has released photo and videos of 2 suspects and is seeking the public's help in identifying them.

Suspects.plaintext:
thumb|right|150px|upright|Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, the younger of the two brothers

In a 5:20 p.m. news conference on April 18, the FBI released photos and a video of two suspects, and sought the public's help in identifying them. According to the FBI, one of the suspects was seen placing a backpack at the scene minutes before the second bomb exploded. 

Authorities identified two brothers as the suspects: 26-year-old Tamerlan Tsarnaev and 19-year-old Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev. Ethnic Chechens from the North Caucasus, the two immigrated to the United States in 2002.  They had been living in Cambridge, Massachusetts, for the prior ten years.  They had previously lived in Tokmok, Kyrgyzstan and Makhachkala, Dagestan, Russia.  Both brothers are Muslims. The brothers' uncle and aunt insisted that the religion  played no role in their motivation for the bombing.

Tamerlan Tsarnaev (October 21, 1986 – April 19, 2013) was killed during a massive manhunt launched in the early hours of April 19. He had been quoted as saying, "I don't have a single American friend, I don't understand them."  He had been arrested in 2009 for domestic assault and battery, after assaulting his girlfriend.  He was not a U.S. citizen, but was a permanent resident. He was born in Russia. 

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev (born July 22, 1993) at the time of the incident was a student at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth, with a major in marine biology.  He was born in Kyrgyzstan.  He became a naturalized U.S. citizen on September 11, 2012.  On television, his uncle pleaded with Dzhokhar to turn himself in. Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev was taken into federal custody after a standoff.

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative [[Peter T. King|Peter King]], member of the [[United States House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence|House Intelligence Committee]] said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."<ref>{{cite web|title=Live updates: Obama calls Boston bombings a 'heinous, cowardly' act of terror |url= http://www.latimes.com/news/nation/nationnow/la-na-nn-boston-searches-for-clues-to-bombing-that-killed-3-injured-176-20130416,0,318317.story?page=2 |work=LA Times|accessdate=April 16, 2013}}</ref>

Murphy]], told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.washingtonpost.com/world/national-security/security-video-may-show-boston-marathon-bomb-suspect-report-of-arrest-premature/2013/04/17/2be1a3f6-a78b-11e2-b029-8fb7e977ef71_story.html|title= Security video may show Boston Marathon bomb suspect; report of arrest premature |author = David Montgomery |author2 = Marc Fisher|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=April 17, 2013|accessdate=April 18, 2013}}</ref> Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.<ref>{{cite news|title=Videos Said to Show Clear Images of 2 Bombing Suspects|url=http://www.nytimes.com/2013/04/19/us/boston-set-to-mourn-bombing-victims.html?hp&_r=0|accessdate=April 18, 2013|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=April 18, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Authorities have clear video images of two suspects|url=http://bostonglobe.com/metro/2013/04/18/authorities-have-clear-video-images-two-suspects/YejgNWAcmChcx2lUXigs5I/story.html|accessdate=April 18, 2013|newspaper=[[The Boston Globe]]|date=April 18, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Video images yield two possible Boston bombing suspects|url=http://www.latimes.com/news/nationworld/nation/la-na-boston-bombings-investigation-20130418,0,2651203.story|accessdate=April 18, 2013|newspaper=[[The Los Angeles Times]]|date=April 18, 2013}}</ref>

===False reports of arrests===
On April 17, false reports that an arrest had been made originated on AP and CNN and were repeated in other media. The FBI issued a statement saying that there had been no arrests and cautioning news outlets not to be reckless, saying "these stories often have unintended consequences".

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

The FBI reports that this pressure cooker fragment is part of one of the explosive devices|thumb|left
A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.

On April 17, false reports that an arrest had been made originated on AP and CNN and were repeated in other media. The FBI issued a statement saying that there had been no arrests and cautioning news outlets not to be reckless, saying "these stories often have unintended consequences".

thumb|right|150px|upright|Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, the younger of the two brothers

In a 5:20 p.m. news conference on April 18, the FBI released photos and a video of two suspects, and sought the public's help in identifying them. According to the FBI, one of the suspects was seen placing a backpack at the scene minutes before the second bomb exploded. 

Authorities identified two brothers as the suspects: 26-year-old Tamerlan Tsarnaev and 19-year-old Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev. Ethnic Chechens from the North Caucasus, the two immigrated to the United States in 2002.  They had been living in Cambridge, Massachusetts, for the prior ten years.  They had previously lived in Tokmok, Kyrgyzstan and Makhachkala, Dagestan, Russia.  Both brothers are Muslims. The brothers' uncle and aunt insisted that the religion  played no role in their motivation for the bombing.

Tamerlan Tsarnaev (October 21, 1986 – April 19, 2013) was killed during a massive manhunt launched in the early hours of April 19. He had been quoted as saying, "I don't have a single American friend, I don't understand them."  He had been arrested in 2009 for domestic assault and battery, after assaulting his girlfriend.  He was not a U.S. citizen, but was a permanent resident. He was born in Russia. 

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev (born July 22, 1993) at the time of the incident was a student at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth, with a major in marine biology.  He was born in Kyrgyzstan.  He became a naturalized U.S. citizen on September 11, 2012.  On television, his uncle pleaded with Dzhokhar to turn himself in. Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev was taken into federal custody after a standoff on April 19.

Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.

Ethnic Chechens from the North Caucasus, the two immigrated to the United States in 2002.  They had been living in Cambridge, Massachusetts, for the prior ten years.  They had previously lived in Tokmok, Kyrgyzstan and Makhachkala, Dagestan, Russia.  Both brothers are Muslims. The brothers' uncle and aunt insisted that the religion  played no role in their motivation for the bombing.

Tamerlan Tsarnaev (October 21, 1986 – April 19, 2013) was killed during a massive manhunt launched in the early hours of April 19. He had been quoted as saying, "I don't have a single American friend, I don't understand them."  He had been arrested in 2009 for domestic assault and battery, after assaulting his girlfriend.  He was not a U.S. citizen, but was a permanent resident. He was born in Russia. 

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev (born July 22, 1993) at the time of the incident was a student at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth, with a major in marine biology.  He was born in Kyrgyzstan.  He became a naturalized U.S. citizen on September 11, 2012.  On television, his uncle pleaded with Dzhokhar to turn himself in. Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev was found and taken into federal custody after a standoff on April 19.

thumb|right|150px|upright|Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, the younger of the two brothers

In a 5:20 p.m. news conference on April 18, the FBI released photos and a video of two suspects, and sought the public's help in identifying them. According to the FBI, one of the suspects was seen placing a backpack at the scene minutes before the second bomb exploded. 

Authorities identified two brothers as the suspects: 26-year-old Tamerlan Tsarnaev and 19-year-old Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev. Ethnic Chechens from the North Caucasus, the two immigrated to the United States in 2002.  They had been living in Cambridge, Massachusetts, for the prior ten years.  They had previously lived in Tokmok, Kyrgyzstan and Makhachkala, Dagestan, Russia.  Both brothers are Muslims. 

Tamerlan Tsarnaev (October 21, 1986 – April 19, 2013) was killed during a massive manhunt launched in the early hours of April 19. He had been quoted as saying, "I don't have a single American friend, I don't understand them."  He had been arrested in 2009 for domestic assault and battery, after assaulting his girlfriend.  He was not a U.S. citizen, but was a permanent resident. He was born in Russia. 

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev (born July 22, 1993) at the time of the incident was a student at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth, with a major in marine biology.  He was born in Kyrgyzstan.  He became a naturalized U.S. citizen on September 11, 2012.  On television, his uncle pleaded with Dzhokhar to turn himself in. He was found and taken into federal custody following a standoff in the evening of April 19.

thumb|Hazmat workers near the scene

The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is investigating the attack along with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Central Intelligence Agency, and the National Counterterrorism Center, is treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, though no perpetrator has officially been identified.

thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media
At a press conference held at 6:00 p.m. on the day of the bombings, Boston police commissioner Edward F. Davis told reporters that no suspect was in custody. Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable". Early in the morning on April 16, law enforcement officials searched a residence in the nearby Boston suburb of Revere, the home of the Saudi man, who had been injured by shrapnel and was considered to be a "person of interest". CNN also reported that the man was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place.  Representative Peter King, member of the House Intelligence Committee said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."

The FBI reports that this pressure cooker fragment is part of one of the explosive devices|thumb|left
A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a pressure cooker packed with shards of metal, nails, and ball bearings to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack. The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop. Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb. Gun powder was most likely used in the explosive devices.

The president of Boston's City Council, Stephen J. Murphy, told reporters on Wednesday, April 17, 2013, that a surveillance tape showing a man depositing a black backpack near the location of the first explosion had been discovered. Authorities have found clear video images (with their faces visible) of two potential suspects carrying black backpacks, one at the scene of each explosion.

False reports of arrests
On April 17, false reports that an arrest had been made originated on AP and CNN and were repeated in other media. The FBI issued a statement saying that there had been no arrests and cautioning news outlets not to be reckless, saying "these stories often have unintended consequences".

thumb|right|150px|upright|Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, the younger of the two brothers

In a 5:20 p.m. news conference on April 18, the FBI released photos and a video of two suspects, and sought the public's help in identifying them. According to the FBI, one of the suspects was seen placing a backpack at the scene minutes before the second bomb exploded. 

Authorities identified two brothers as the suspects: 26-year-old Tamerlan Tsarnaev and 19-year-old Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev. Ethnic Chechens from the North Caucasus, the two immigrated to the United States in 2002.  They had been living in Cambridge, Massachusetts, for the prior ten years.  They had previously lived in Tokmok, Kyrgyzstan and Makhachkala, Dagestan, Russia.  Both brothers are Muslims. A YouTube account in Tamerlan's name featured two videos about terrorism, and Tamerlan's aunt said that in recent years, he had become increasingly observant and began praying five times a day. 

Tamerlan Tsarnaev (October 21, 1986 – April 19, 2013) was killed during a massive manhunt launched in the early hours of April 19. He had been quoted as saying, "I don't have a single American friend, I don't understand them."  He had been arrested in 2009 for domestic assault and battery, after assaulting his girlfriend.  He was not a U.S. citizen, but was a permanent resident. He was born in Russia. 

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev (born July 22, 1993) at the time of the incident was a student at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth, with a major in marine biology.  He was born in Kyrgyzstan.  He became a naturalized U.S. citizen on September 11, 2012.  On television, his uncle pleaded with Dzhokhar to turn himself in. He was found and taken into federal custody following a standoff in the evening of April 19.

Suspects.plaintext:
thumb|right|150px|upright|Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, the younger of the two brothers

In a 5:20 p.m. news conference on April 18, the FBI released photos and a video of two suspects, and sought the public's help in identifying them. According to the FBI, one of the suspects was seen placing a backpack at the scene minutes before the second bomb exploded. 

Authorities identified two brothers as the suspects: 26-year-old Tamerlan Tsarnaev and 19-year-old Dzhokhar A. Tsarnaev. Ethnic Chechens from the North Caucasus, the two immigrated to the United States in 2002.  They had been living in Cambridge, Massachusetts, for the prior ten years.  They had previously lived in Tokmok, Kyrgyzstan and Makhachkala, Dagestan, Russia.  Both brothers are Muslims. A YouTube account in Tamerlan's name featured two radical Islamist videos, and Tamerlan's aunt said that in recent years, he had become increasingly observant and began praying five times a day. He told a photographer: ""God said no alcohol. There are no values anymore… people can't control themselves."  

Tamerlan Tsarnaev (October 21, 1986 – April 19, 2013) was killed during a massive manhunt launched in the early hours of April 19. He had been quoted as saying, "I don't have a single American friend, I don't understand them."  He had been arrested in 2009 for domestic assault and battery, after assaulting his girlfriend.  He was not a U.S. citizen, but was a permanent resident. He was born in Russia. 

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev (born July 22, 1993) at the time of the incident was a student at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth, with a major in marine biology.  He was born in Kyrgyzstan.   He became a naturalized U.S. citizen on September 11, 2012.  On television, his uncle pleaded with Dzhokhar to turn himself in. He was found and taken into federal custody following a standoff in the evening of April 19.

Investigation.wikitext:
[[File:Hazmat biohazard team at Boston Marathon near the finish line 07.jpeg|thumb|[[Dangerous goods|Hazmat]] workers near the scene]]
The [[Federal Bureau of Investigation]], which has been investigating the attack along with the [[Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives]] (ATF), the [[Central Intelligence Agency]], and the [[National Counterterrorism Center]],<ref name="Hosenball">{{cite web| url=http://www.globalpost.com/dispatch/news/thomson-reuters/130415/investigators-scour-video-photos-boston-marathon-bomb-clues |title=Investigators scour video, photos for Boston Marathon bomb clues|last1=Hosenball| first1=Mark |first2=Svea| last2=Herbst-Bayliss |date=April 16, 2013|work=[[GlobalPost]]|publisher=[[Thomson Reuters]] |accessdate=April 16, 2013}}</ref> was treating the bombings as a terrorist attack, with at least two alleged perpetrators so far having been officially identified.<ref name="Fox News1"/><ref>{{Citation | url = http://www.nytimes.com/2013/04/19/us/fbi-releases-video-of-boston-bombing-suspects.html?pagewanted=all&_r=0 | title = FBI Posts Images of Pair Suspected in Boston Attack | newspaper = The NY Times | accessdate = April 19, 2013}}</ref>

United States government officials stated that there had been no intelligence reports that indicated such a bombing would take place. Representative [[Peter T. King|Peter King]], member of the [[United States House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence|House Intelligence Committee]] said: "I received two top secret briefings last week on the current threat levels in the United States, and there was no evidence of this at all."<ref>{{cite web|title=Live updates: Obama calls Boston bombings a 'heinous, cowardly' act of terror |url=http://www.latimes.com/news/nation/nationnow/la-na-nn-boston-searches-for-clues-to-bombing-that-killed-3-injured-176-20130416,0,318317.story?page=2 |work=LA Times|accessdate=April 16, 2013}}</ref>
[[File:FBI and JTTF at Boston bombing.jpg|thumb|Richard DesLauriers, special agent in charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, addresses the media.]]

Though not treated as suspects, several people who were near the scene of the blast and the surrounding area were taken into custody and questioned about the bombings, including a Saudi man that police stopped as he was walking away from the explosion, and detained when some of his responses to questions "made them uncomfortable".<ref>{{cite web|title=Injured Saudi man not a suspect in Boston attacks|url=http://www.cbsnews.com/8301-201_162-57579893/sources-injured-saudi-man-not-a-suspect-in-boston-attacks/|last=Sison |first=Bree|publisher=CBS News|accessdate=April 17, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Nelson|first=Steven|title=Boston Police: 'We Are Questioning Many People'|url=http://www.usnews.com/news/newsgram/articles/2013/04/15/boston-police-we-are-questioning-many-people |accessdate=April 16, 2013|newspaper=[[U.S. News & World Report]]}}</ref><ref name="Hunter">{{cite web|url= http://livewire.talkingpointsmemo.com/entry/boston-police-commissioner-there-is-no-suspect-in|title=Boston Police Commissioner: 'There Is No Suspect In Custody'|last=Hunter|first=Walker|date=April 16, 2013|publisher=[[Talking Points Memo]]|accessdate=April 16, 2013}}</ref>  Law enforcement searched his residence in a Boston suburb, but CNN later reported that he was found to have no connection to the attack, with an unnamed U.S. official saying "he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time."<ref name="CNN_FBI">{{cite news|title=FBI will try to rebuild Boston bombs|url=http://edition.cnn.com/2013/04/15/us/boston-marathon-investigation/index.html|last=Smith |first=Matt|coauthors=Josh Levs|publisher=CNN|accessdate=April 17, 2013}}</ref><ref name="Fox News1"/><ref>{{cite news|title=Large police presence in Revere connected to Boston bombing|url=http://www.myfoxboston.com/story/21986273/large-police-presence-in-revere-connected-to-boston-bombing |publisher=[[WFXT]]|accessdate=April 16, 2013}}</ref>
[[File:Pressure cooker bomb.jpg|The FBI reports that this pressure cooker fragment is part of one of the explosive devices.|thumb|left]]

A person who was briefed on the investigation said at least one of the devices was made from a [[pressure cooker]] packed with shards of metal, nails and bearing balls to inflict maximum casualties and was placed in a backpack.<ref name="CNN_FBI"/> The lid of one pressure cooker was found on a nearby rooftop.<ref>{{cite news|last=Ellement|first=John|title=Boston Medical Center reports five-year-old boy in critical condition, 23 victims treated from Boston Marathon bombings|url=http://www.boston.com/metrodesk/2013/04/17/boston-medical-center-reports-five-year-old-boy-critical-condition-victims-treated-from-boston-marathon-bombings/gkKXBTqL2jyNhsC2Kz5GyO/story.html|accessdate=April 17, 2013|newspaper=The Boston Globe|date=April 17, 2013|author2=Brian Ballou}}</ref> Investigators have found remains of an electronic circuit board that was possibly used in the timer of the bomb.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.cbsnews.com/8301-201_162-57579766/boston-marathon-bombings-suburban-apartment-searched/ |title=FBI seeks images in Boston Marathon bomb probe; new details emerge on explosives |work=CBS News|date=April 16, 2013|accessdate=April 16, 2013}}</ref> [[Gunpowder]] was most likely used in the explosive devices.<ref name="Lister">{{cite web|url=http://edition.cnn.com/2013/04/16/us/boston-marathon-lone-wolf/|title=Boston Marathon bombs similar to 'lone wolf' devices, experts say|last=Lister|first=Tim|coauthors=Paul Cruickshank|date=April 17, 2013|work=[[CNN]]|accessdate=April 17, 2013}}</ref>
